title: The covenant prayer
hookLine: Methodists renew their covenant each year: I am no longer my own, but yours

cards: Joshua, old now, gathers the tribes of Israel at Shechem. He reminds them of everything God has done, and then he puts it to them plainly: choose whom you will serve.

And he answers first, for himself: "as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD." The people answer too, and that day, the book says, Joshua made a covenant with them. A promise already made, made again.
Methodists do something like that once a year, at a covenant service, renewing their promise to God in words that aren't easy to say.

teach.b: Covenant is a word the Bible keeps coming back to. In Hebrew it's berit, and it runs from Noah to Abraham to Sinai.

Jeremiah looks ahead to a new one, where God says, "I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people." Not carved on stone this time.
Written inside. John Wesley took up a yearly renewal of that covenant from Puritan writers before him, and gave it to the Methodists. The prayer Methodists say today is short, and it's hard.
It begins with today's line: I am no longer my own, but yours. Then it hands everything over, the pleasant and the painful together.

teach.h: DOING OR SUFFERING, FULL OR EMPTY.
teach.b: Put me to doing, or to suffering. Use me, or set me aside. Let me be full, or empty.
Let me have all things, or nothing. It isn't asking for suffering. It's refusing to make faithfulness depend on comfort.
Plenty of promises come with conditions; this one tries to have none.
Paul gives the ground for it: "ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price." Christian teaching reads that price as Christ's own life. And the prayer doesn't end in loss.
At the close, the one who gave everything away hears that God is theirs too, like the Song of Songs: "My beloved is mine, and I am his." Why say it every year? Because people drift.
A covenant, like a marriage, gets spoken again so it isn't forgotten.

how: Methodists hold a covenant service once a year, often around the new year, where the congregation renews its covenant with God and prays the covenant prayer together.

o: a Methodist prayer yielding everything to God each year
a Methodist prayer asking God to bless their plans
a wedding vow said by a couple before a pastor

p: as for me and my house

s: the covenant prayer asks God only for good things
it offers both: doing and suffering, being used and set aside, full and empty.
Joshua led the people in making a covenant at Shechem

Wesley made up the covenant renewal from nothing

games.q: you're at a covenant service. the prayer offers God your plenty and your emptiness alike. what does it hold back?
games.why: nothing. it hands over the pleasant and the painful together, and then turns around: the one who gave everything hears that God is theirs too.

practice: Notice what you'd find hardest to hand over: a plan, a comfort, a person, being needed. Don't argue with it; just see it.
If you pray, say the prayer's first line slowly, I am no longer my own, but yours, and stop there; if you don't, name the thing once, quietly, and let it sit there without grabbing it back.

wordCard.voice: The covenant prayer. The Methodist prayer of yielding everything to God, said each year when the covenant is renewed.

orig.note: Hebrew: covenant — the word in Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant.

carryVoice: Your line: no longer my own. Full or empty, the promise holds. See you at the table tomorrow.
